read.sections.0.text.source:
A house is a place to live, but its design can also express how people are related to each other. Rooms, materials and decoration may reflect work, family ties, beliefs and the resources people had. A photograph shows some features. To understand what they mean, we also need to know about the people and the particular building.

In South Sulawesi, Indonesia, tongkonan are ancestral houses linked with Toraja communities. Ancestral means connected with earlier generations of a family or community. Raised floors, timber frames and curved roofs make these houses easy to recognise. Yet each house belongs to a larger setting. Indonesia's description of traditional Toraja villages includes houses, granaries (rice stores), farmland and places for the community and its ceremonies. Each village keeps its own mix of these. No single village is repeated everywhere.

This is a highland setting on Sulawesi. It is a different island from Java, where the batiks in Lesson 2 were made. Village life joined rice fields and granaries with spaces for family gatherings and ceremonies. At Nanggala, houses and granaries face each other across an open space where people gather. This shows why a roof alone is not the whole architecture. Architecture is the design and building of places. The way buildings stand together also helps organise a community's life. A Toraja example should not stand for all housing in Indonesia.
read.sections.0.text.back:

read.sections.1.text.source:
Indonesia's national museum, the Museum Nasional Indonesia, explains that a tongkonan is linked with family talks and customary affairs. These are matters guided by a community's long-standing rules. The museum describes three parts: the area below the floor, the main living space and the roof. Each part can carry meaning as well as having a practical use. So architecture organises social life, not just empty space inside walls.

Carving also matters. The museum describes carved walls, doors, windows and roof supports. It explains that some motifs, or repeated designs, are linked to social rank and customary rules. Ornament here is decoration that can also carry meaning. It would be wrong to think that every design is only decoration, or that every house may use every motif. We can describe a carved pattern from a photograph. But we should not invent its meaning because it looks like something we know. Family ties and differences in rank matter to the explanation.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Indonesia's national museum, the Museum Nasional Indonesia, explains that a tongkonan is linked with family discussions and customary affairs. These affairs are matters guided by a community's old rules. The museum describes three parts: the space below the floor, the main living space and the roof. Each part can carry meaning besides having a practical use. So architecture organises social life, not merely empty space inside walls.

Carving is also important. The museum describes carved walls, doors, windows and roof supports. The museum explains that some motifs, that is repeated designs, are linked with social rank and customary rules. Ornament here is decoration that can also carry meaning. We would be wrong to think that every design is only decoration, or that every house may use every motif. We can describe a carved pattern from a photograph. But we should not make up its meaning only because it looks like something we know. Family ties and differences in rank are important for the explanation.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Customary" is "adat", the word Malaysian and Indonesian communities both use for customary law and affairs. "Ornament" is "ornamen" (glossary).

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Indonesia's national museum says a tongkonan is linked to family talks. It is also linked to customary matters. These are things the group decides by its old rules. The museum names three parts. There is the space under the floor, the main room and the roof. Each part has a use, and it can have a meaning too. So a house helps shape how people live together.

Carving matters too. Walls, doors, windows and roof posts are carved. The museum says some designs are linked to a family's rank. They also follow the group's rules. This kind of ornament is decoration with a meaning. Not every house may use every design. We can describe a carved pattern from a photo. But we should not guess its meaning. It may only look like something we know.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Particular buildings and a living heritage
read.sections.2.heading.back: Particular buildings and a living heritage

read.sections.2.text.source:
The two photographs show particular buildings in the Toraja region at particular times. They let us see roofs, repeated shapes and the posts and beams that form each building's structure. We can also see how the buildings stand in relation to each other. But the photographs do not tell us who lived in each room, or what all Toraja people believe today. An ancestral house can matter to many people without being a full picture of family life today.

Heritage is living. People look after buildings, replace materials, change spaces and decide how traditions continue. Living heritage means places and ways of life that people inherit and still use and change. The 2009 submission about the villages describes places that had already changed, not a landscape kept outside history. Studying a tongkonan connects architecture with skilled work, land, family knowledge and earlier generations. It also shows something useful. A building's importance can reach beyond whoever lives in it, because other people see their own connections in the place.
read.sections.2.text.back:
The two photographs show particular buildings in the Toraja region at particular times. The pictures let us see roofs, repeated shapes and the posts and beams that form each building's structure. We can also see the position of the buildings in relation to each other. But the photographs do not tell us who lived in each room, or what all Toraja people believe today. An ancestral house can be important to many people without being a full picture of family life today.

Heritage is alive. People look after buildings, replace materials, change spaces and decide how traditions continue. Living heritage means places and ways of life that people inherit and still use and change. The 2009 proposal about the villages describes places that had already changed, not a landscape kept outside history. Studying a tongkonan connects architecture with skilled work, land, family knowledge and earlier generations. It also shows something useful. A building's importance can reach beyond the people who live in it, because other people see their own connections with the place.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Submission" (to UNESCO's Tentative List) is "cadangan" (proposal), matching educatorNotes.2.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
The two photos show some buildings at certain times. We can see roofs, posts and shapes that repeat. The posts and frame are the structure that holds a house up. We can see how the houses stand together. But the photos do not show who lived in each room. They do not show what all Toraja people believe today.

This is living heritage. People still use these places, and they change them. They fix the houses and put in new parts. They decide how the old ways go on. A report from 2009 says the villages had already changed. A tongkonan links building skills, land, family and people of the past. It can matter to many people. It is not only for the people who live in it.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:

We can see how the houses stand together. But the pictures do not show who lived in each room. The pictures do not show what all Toraja people believe today.

This is living heritage. People still use these places, and they change them. They repair the houses and put in new parts. They decide how the old ways continue. A report from 2009 says the villages had already changed. A tongkonan connects building skills, land, family and people of the past. It can be important to many people. It is not only for the people who live in it.

write.example.back: One feature I can see is the carving on the walls and posts of the house near Rantepao. The museum says some carved designs are linked with a family's rank and community rules. I would need to ask and learn more.

visual.alt.source: Toraja houses with tall roofs that curve up at both ends like boats stand in two rows facing each other across an open grassy space. The houses are raised on wooden posts, with carved and painted walls, and a carved post at the front of the nearest house.
visual.alt.back: Toraja houses with tall roofs that curve upward at both ends like boats stand in two rows, facing each other across an open grassy area. The houses are raised on wooden posts, with carved and painted walls, and a carved post in front of the nearest house.

visual.caption.back: Tongkonan houses at Kete Kesu, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, photographed in 2011. One view of one village at one time.

secondVisual.alt.source: A tall Toraja house whose roof sweeps up steeply at the front, covered in metal sheets. The carved and painted front rests on wooden posts, with a tall carved post in front. Lower houses with metal roofs stand beside it, with washing hung on a line.
secondVisual.alt.back: A tall Toraja house with a roof that rises steeply at the front, covered with zinc sheets. Its carved and painted front rests on wooden posts, with a tall carved post in front of it. Lower houses with zinc roofs stand beside it, with clothes hung on a line.
secondVisual.alt.note: "Metal sheets" is "kepingan zink", the everyday Malaysian name for corrugated metal roofing.

A Toraja example does not stand for all housing in Indonesia. Keep the pattern a learner can see apart from what a source says it means, and don't invent meanings for carved motifs.
